title: Ancient philosophy
audience: a college student in a philosophy degree program, or an adult studying the same material on their own
purpose: Read the founders of Western philosophy in translation: the Presocratics on change and being, Socrates and the Sophists, Plato on the Forms, knowledge, the soul and justice, Aristotle on logic, substance, the four causes, the soul and the good life, and the Hellenistic schools (Epicureans, Stoics and Skeptics).
primary_reading: The Internet Classics Archive (MIT): Greek and Roman texts in translation (free)

weeks.1: The first philosophers: Thales to Heraclitus
weeks.2: Parmenides, Zeno and the problem of change
weeks.4: Socrates: questioning, virtue and the examined life
weeks.5: Plato: the Forms and the divided line
weeks.6: Plato: knowledge, recollection and the soul
weeks.10: Aristotle: the four causes, nature and the soul
weeks.12: Hellenistic philosophy: Epicureans, Stoics and Skeptics

blocks.deliverable: Reconstruct one of Zeno's paradoxes and a reply.
Analyze a Socratic definition and its refutation.
Explain the allegory of the cave in terms of the theory of Forms.
Week 7 midterm; reconstruct an argument from the Republic.
Apply the four causes to three examples.
Compare the Epicurean and Stoic views of death.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Ancient metaphysics essay: write a 2,000-word essay comparing Plato's and Aristotle's answers to one question (what is most real, what explains change, or what the soul is), using passages from public-domain translations, and evaluate which answer better handles one objection.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
